
## S3.2 Random curve effect, GLS and curve bootstrap

```{r s4-2}
cdep <- CMP |> filter(source == "synthetic", error != "iid") |>
  group_by(cell, estimand) |>
  mutate(wr = width / width[arm == "reml_cl2"], sr = score / score[arm == "reml_cl2"]) |> ungroup()
cd <- \(a, e = "beta", col = "coverage") cdep[[col]][cdep$arm %in% a & cdep$estimand == e]
pcre_t <- CMPF$time[CMPF$arm == "PCRE"]
gm_est <- \(fit, set, e = ESTIMAND_LABELS[["beta"]]) comp_est$mse_vs_NCV[comp_est$fit == fit & comp_est$setting == set & comp_est$estimand == e]
```

Three further methods address dependent residual curves. All are fitted to the same data as the
study's REML fit, with common random numbers, in the `r n_distinct(cdep$cell)` Gaussian
main-factorial settings with dependent errors at the default signal (rough stationary and smooth
errors, $G = 40$ and 100; below: the *four synthetic Gaussian settings with dependent errors*), in the corresponding
settings with independent errors, and in the six plasmode datasets with independent source curves (observed curves independent across subjects; midpoint
truth, i.e. smoothing parameters at the geometric mean of the REML and NCV values; REML residuals;
all subjects and 40: `r n_distinct(CMP$cell[CMP$source == "plasmode"])`
plasmode combinations). The evidence on these methods is limited to these four Gaussian settings
with dependent errors and these plasmode combinations.

*Functional random effect per curve* (`pcre()` in refund): the REML model plus a curve-level random
function expanded in the leading eigenfunctions of the REML residual curves (95% of their variance),
with model-based intervals.

*Generalized least squares (GLS).* Estimate the within-curve residual covariance from the REML
residual curves, either as their raw covariance or as an FPCA estimate plus white noise; prewhiten
every curve with the inverse square root of that covariance; refit by REML; use model-based
intervals. This procedure is the algorithm of refund's former `pffr_gls()`, rebuilt from refund's internal
functions; a singular estimated covariance (fewer curves than grid points) is repaired by the nearest
positive-definite matrix.

*Curve bootstrap*: resample whole curves, refit by REML (199 resamples), and form percentile intervals
or Wald intervals with the bootstrap standard error around the REML estimate.

*Results.* In the four synthetic Gaussian settings with dependent errors, the random curve effect and GLS with
the FPCA covariance cover $\beta(s,t)$ at `r rng(cd(c("pcre", "gls_fpc")))`, at
`r rng(cd(c("pcre", "gls_fpc"), col = "wr"), 2)` times REML + CL2's width and
`r rng(cd(c("pcre", "gls_fpc"), col = "sr"), 2)` times its interval score. The random curve effect
undercovers the mean and $\alpha(t)$ there: it covers the mean at `r rng(cd("pcre", "mean"))` and
$\alpha(t)$ at `r rng(cd("pcre", "alpha"))`. On the plasmode data, both methods fall to
`r rng(c(cmp_cv("pcre", "beta", "plasmode"), cmp_cv("gls_fpc", "beta", "plasmode")))` for $\beta$, while
REML + CL2 covers `r rng(cmp_cv("reml_cl2", "beta", "plasmode"))`. A common working covariance that
fits the synthetic error processes is only an approximation to the subject-specific two-point error
law of the plasmode generator (each subject's error is plus or minus its own residual curve; S2), and the model-based intervals of these fits do not hold their
level there; this finding concerns that generator and is not a general statement about real data.

GLS with the raw covariance undercovers everywhere
(`r rng(cmp_cv("gls_raw", "beta", "synthetic, independent"))` even under independent errors), because
the raw covariance of fewer curves than grid points is a poor, singular estimate. The percentile
bootstrap covers $\beta$ at `r rng(cmp_cv("boot_pct", "beta", "plasmode"))` on the plasmode data with
intervals `r f(geo(comp_cov$width_rel[comp_cov$arm == CMP_ARMS[["boot_pct"]] & comp_cov$estimand == ESTIMAND_LABELS[["beta"]] & comp_cov$setting == "plasmode"]), 2)`
times as wide as REML + CL2's, at the cost of 199 refits (Appendix C of the paper).

*As estimators*, the random curve effect and GLS (FPCA) remove most of REML's excess error. Their mean squared error
for $\beta$ relative to the NCV fit's (geometric mean over settings) is
`r f(gm_est("pcre", "synthetic, dependent"), 2)` and `r f(gm_est("GLS (FPCA cov.)", "synthetic, dependent"), 2)`
in the four synthetic Gaussian settings with dependent errors (REML `r f(gm_est("REML", "synthetic, dependent"), 1)`),
and `r f(gm_est("pcre", "plasmode"), 2)` and `r f(gm_est("GLS (FPCA cov.)", "plasmode"), 2)` on the
plasmode datasets (REML `r f(gm_est("REML", "plasmode"), 2)`; per setting `r rng(cmp_er("pcre", "beta", "plasmode"))`
and `r rng(cmp_er("GLS (FPCA cov.)", "beta", "plasmode"))`). Both thus improve much on REML, but, in the
synthetic settings, they are worse than NCV. Their plasmode advantage over NCV rests on the midpoint
truth with REML residuals only. The GLS covariance is estimated from the residual curves of a REML
pilot fit to each simulated dataset; because these errors are sign-flipped REML residuals of the
original fit, those pilot residuals closely resemble the curves that generate them. The random curve effect is expensive:
median `r f(median(pcre_t), 0)` s per fit including the REML pilot fit, up to `r f(max(pcre_t), 0)` s, against
`r f(median(CMPF$time[CMPF$arm == "REML"]), 1)` s for REML.

```{r f-s4-cmp}
#| fig-cap: "Random curve effect (pcre), GLS and curve bootstrap: grid-averaged coverage per setting or plasmode combination (one circle each, jittered vertically; bar: median), by estimand and data source. Dashed: nominal 0.95."
#| fig-height: 5.6
sfig_strip(FIGS[["comparators-coverage"]], coverage, "coverage (grid average)", LEVEL, FALSE, seq(0, 1, 0.2), "arm")
```

```{r f-s4-cmp-est}
#| fig-cap: "Mean squared error of each estimator divided by that of the NCV fit, per setting or plasmode combination (one circle each, jittered vertically; bar: median; log scale; below 1 = better than NCV). The bootstrap intervals use the REML estimate."
#| fig-height: 5
sfig_strip(FIGS[["comparators-estimation"]], vs_NCV, "MSE / MSE of the NCV fit (log scale)", 1, TRUE, c(0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10), "fit")
```

```{r t-s4-cmp-cov}
#| output: asis
stab(comp_cov |> mutate(setting = recode(setting, `synthetic, dependent` = "syn. dep.", `synthetic, independent` = "syn. indep.")) |> rename(settings = cells, `width rel.` = width_rel, `IS rel.` = score_rel),
  "Comparators: mean and minimum coverage, mean 5% quantile of pointwise coverage, width and interval score relative to REML + CL2 (geometric means of per-setting ratios).", digits = 2, font = 6, long = TRUE)
```

```{r t-s4-cmp-est}
#| output: asis
stab(comp_est |> mutate(setting = recode(setting, `synthetic, dependent` = "syn. dep.", `synthetic, independent` = "syn. indep.")) |> rename(settings = cells),
  "Comparators as estimators: median relative error, MSE relative to REML and to NCV (geometric means of per-setting ratios; range for NCV).", digits = 2, font = 6, long = TRUE)
```

*CL2 on the GLS and random-curve-effect fits.* GLS whitens each curve with $\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}^{-1/2}$. The
transform acts within curves, so curves stay independent clusters, and CL2 (Bayesian form, curves as
clusters) applies to the whitened fit; it does not need $\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}$ to be correct.
GLS-FPCA + CL2 is CL2 on the GLS fit with the FPCA covariance, pcre + CL2 is CL2 on the fit with the
random curve effect (`pcre()`). The comparison uses replicates 1--100, where all constructions
exist; one pcre + CL2 replicate failed in a singular value decomposition and is left out for that
construction only. The eigenvalue floor of the leverage adjustment (Appendix A.2 of the paper) bound in no
GLS fit and, among the pcre fits, only on the running data, there in `r floor_tab$floored[1]` of
`r floor_tab$reps[1]` replicates with all subjects and in `r floor_tab$floored[2]` of `r floor_tab$reps[2]`
with 40, so pcre + CL2 on that dataset depends on the floor. In the four synthetic Gaussian settings with dependent errors, GLS-FPCA + CL2 covers $\beta(s,t)$ at
`r f(cav("gls_fpc_cl2", "synthetic, dependent"), 2)`, at `r f(cav("gls_fpc_cl2", "synthetic, dependent", "width_rel"), 2)`
times REML + CL2's width (interval score `r f(cav("gls_fpc_cl2", "synthetic, dependent", "score_rel"), 2)`
times). On the plasmode data, it covers $\beta$ at `r f(cav("gls_fpc_cl2", "plasmode"), 2)` (by dataset
`r rng(ca_pm_app$v)`; GLS-FPCA without CL2 `r f(cav("gls_fpc", "plasmode"), 2)`, REML + CL2
`r f(cav("reml_cl2", "plasmode"), 2)`), at `r f(cav("gls_fpc_cl2", "plasmode", "width_rel"), 2)` times
the width. The standard error of GLS-FPCA + CL2 is close to the spread of the GLS estimate there (geometric mean
SE/SD `r f(geo(CA_se$se_sd_ratio), 2)`). This agreement is consistent with residual smoothing bias of the GLS
estimate under the plasmode generator, but an aggregate ratio near one does not exclude local or
tail errors of the standard error, and no single cause is established. pcre + CL2 behaves alike ($\beta$
`r f(cav("pcre_cl2", "plasmode"), 2)`) and repairs the model-based intervals of the random curve effect for $\alpha(t)$ on synthetic data
(`r f(cav("pcre", "synthetic, dependent", "coverage", "alpha"), 2)` to
`r f(cav("pcre_cl2", "synthetic, dependent", "coverage", "alpha"), 2)`). GLS with the raw residual
covariance fails with CL2 as well (`r f(cav("gls_raw_cl2", "synthetic, dependent"), 2)` under dependent
synthetic errors): with more grid points than curves, the raw covariance absorbs the residuals
themselves.

```{r t-s3-cl2-arms}
#| output: asis
stab(ca_tab |> mutate(setting = recode(setting, `synthetic, dependent` = "syn. dep.", `synthetic, independent` = "syn. indep.")) |>
  rename(`min cov.` = cov_min, `width rel.` = width_rel, `IS rel.` = score_rel, `MSE/NCV` = mse_vs_NCV),
  "CL2 on the GLS and pcre fits (replicates 1--100): mean and minimum coverage over settings or plasmode combinations, mean 5% quantile of pointwise coverage, width and interval score relative to REML + CL2, MSE relative to the NCV fit (geometric means), and detection rate, by data source, estimand and construction.", digits = 2, font = 6, long = TRUE)
```

{{< include supp/_s4-fgee.qmd >}}

# S4 Intervals centered at the NCV fit and smoothing-parameter terms {#sec-s5}

This section collects approaches that did not work: intervals centered at the curve-blocked NCV
estimate, a corrected version of mgcv's neighborhood covariance for NCV fits, and a
smoothing-parameter uncertainty term for REML + CL2. Each approach is given as method, derivation, result and reason. The notation is that of §2 and
Appendix A of the paper: $\mathbf W$ holds the working weights including $1/\phi$,
$\mathbf S = \sum_k(\lambda_k/\phi)\mathbf S_k$, $\mathbf V_p = (\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X + \mathbf S)^{-1}$
and $\mathbf V_e = \mathbf V_p\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\mathbf V_p$. In addition,
$\mathbf F = \mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X + \mathbf S = \mathbf V_p^{-1}$ is the penalized Hessian,
$\boldsymbol\rho = \log\boldsymbol\lambda$ and $\dot{\mathbf S}_k = \partial\mathbf S/\partial\rho_k = (\lambda_k/\phi)\mathbf S_k$.
For a canonical link, the working weights are $w_{ij} = (d\mu/d\eta)_{ij}/\phi$, and the score of curve
$i$ is $\mathbf u_i = \mathbf X_i^\top(\mathbf y_i - \boldsymbol\mu_i)/\phi$. The CL2 influence of
curve $i$ is $\mathbf k_i = \mathbf V_p\mathbf U_i$ with $\mathbf U_i$ as in Appendix A, so that
$\hat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{CL2}} = \mathbf V_f + (\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)$ with the frequentist form
$\mathbf V_f = \frac{G}{G-1}\sum_i\mathbf k_i\mathbf k_i^\top$. $\mathbf L$ maps the coefficients to an
estimand's values on its grid.

```{r s4-lambda-spread}
# sampling spread and mgcv's estimated SD of log lambda-hat for the surface penalty along s
# (REML, dependent main-factorial settings)
lcc <- readr::read_csv("lambda-correction/summaries/lc-calib.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::filter(error != "iid", grepl("L.X1$", par))
lcc_sd <- with(dplyr::filter(lcc, source == "ij"), tapply(mc_sd, G, mean))
lcc_shrink <- lcc_sd[["100"]] / lcc_sd[["40"]]
lcc_naive <- with(dplyr::filter(lcc, source == "naive"), median_est_sd / mc_sd)
```

## S4.1 Intervals centered at the NCV fit

Under dependent errors, curve-blocked NCV estimates $\beta(s,t)$ with a fraction of REML's error (S1.6),
but NCV + CL2 undercovers. This section gives diagnostics for why it undercovers and evaluates six constructions that try to repair it. None of the
constructions as implemented here gives intervals around the NCV estimate that hold their level
across the plasmode datasets; the conclusions refer to these constructions, not to every possible
correction.

### (a) Why NCV + CL2 undercovers

*Method.* We use two diagnostics. *Bias-eliminated coverage* replaces each interval's center by the
estimate minus its pointwise bias (estimated from the replicates) and shows the coverage without
bias. A refit with every smoothing parameter fixed at the median NCV value of its plasmode combination removes
the variability of the selected smoothing parameters. It also moves every replicate to the typical
amount of smoothing, so it changes the bias as well as the variability; it uses the replicates
themselves and is a diagnostic, not a decomposition of the shortfall and not a method.

*Result.* In the synthetic settings with dependent errors at $G = 100$, NCV + CL2 covers $\beta$ at
`r f(dsv("smooth truth", "ncv_cl2", "cov"), 2)` (smooth truth) and `r f(dsv("rough truth", "ncv_cl2", "cov"), 2)`
(rough truth); without bias, it would cover `r f(dsv("smooth truth", "ncv_cl2", "be"), 2)` and
`r f(dsv("rough truth", "ncv_cl2", "be"), 2)`. On the six plasmode datasets with independent source curves (observed curves independent across subjects), the
ratio of the root mean square standard error to the replicate SD of the estimate (SE/SD, median over
grid points) is `r rng(dpv("ncv_cl2", "se_sd"))` for NCV + CL2; with fixed smoothing parameters, it is
`r rng(dpv("ncvfix_cl2", "se_sd"))`, but coverage stays at `r rng(dpv("ncvfix_cl2", "cov"))`.

*Reason.* On synthetic data, the shortfall is mainly smoothing bias at the amount of smoothing NCV
selects. On the plasmode data, the diagnostics suggest two contributions: the standard error is short,
consistent with the variability of the selected smoothing parameters that it ignores, and coverage
stays short at a fixed typical amount of smoothing, consistent with smoothing bias. Fixing the
smoothing parameters changes both the center and its sampling distribution, so the two cannot be
separated exactly.

```{r t-s5-diag}
#| output: asis
stab(diag_p_tab, "Plasmode, $\\beta(s,t)$, all subjects: coverage (5% quantile of pointwise coverage) and SE/SD for NCV + CL2, its bias-eliminated coverage, NCV + CL2 after a refit at the median NCV smoothing parameters, and REML + CL2 (100 replicates per combination).", font = 7)
```

### (b) Widening by the NCV--REML difference

*Method.* Widen the NCV + CL2 interval in quadrature by the difference of the two estimates,
$\mathbf L\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_N \pm z\{\mathrm{se}^2_{\mathrm{CL2},N} + (\mathbf L\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_N - \mathbf L\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_R)^2\}^{1/2}$,
with the difference standing in for the bias of the NCV estimate. If the bias $b$ were known, an
interval $\pm z(\sigma^2 + b^2)^{1/2}$ would never undercover at the 95% level:

```{r s5-rss}
s1_cov <- \(r, z) pnorm(r - z * sqrt(1 + r^2)) + pnorm(-r - z * sqrt(1 + r^2)) # non-coverage
s1_r <- c(seq(1e-3, 1, by = 1e-3), seq(1.01, 50, by = 0.01))
s1_dip <- \(z) max(s1_cov(s1_r, z)) - 2 * pnorm(-z)
stopifnot(
  s1_dip(qnorm(0.975)) <= 0, s1_dip(sqrt(3) + 1e-3) <= 0, s1_dip(sqrt(3) - 1e-3) > 0,
  abs((2 * pnorm(-1.96) - s1_cov(0.01, 1.96)) / 0.01^4 - 1.96 * (1.96^2 - 3) * dnorm(1.96) / 6) < 1e-3
)
```

with $r = b/\sigma$, its coverage is $c(r) = \Phi\{z(1 + r^2)^{1/2} - r\} - \Phi\{-z(1 + r^2)^{1/2} - r\}$,
and $c(r) - c(0) = z(z^2 - 3)\varphi(z)r^4/6 + O(r^6)$. Numerically, $c(r) \ge c(0)$ for every $r$
exactly when $z \ge \sqrt 3$, that is for nominal levels of at least
`r f(2 * pnorm(sqrt(3)) - 1, 3)`.

*Derivation.* The interval covers when $|Z + r| \le z(1 + r^2)^{1/2}$ with $Z \sim N(0, 1)$. Write
$u = z(1 + r^2)^{1/2} = z + zr^2/2 - zr^4/8 + O(r^6)$. Since $\Phi(-u - r) = 1 - \Phi(u + r)$,
$$
c(r) = \Phi(u - r) + \Phi(u + r) - 1 = 2\Phi(u) - 1 + \varphi'(u)\,r^2 + \varphi'''(u)\,r^4/12 + O(r^6),
$$
an even function of $r$. With $\varphi'(z) = -z\varphi(z)$, $\varphi''(z) = (z^2 - 1)\varphi(z)$ and
$\varphi'''(z) = (3z - z^3)\varphi(z)$, expanding $u$ around $z$ gives
$2\Phi(u) = 2\Phi(z) + z\varphi(z)r^2 - (z + z^3)\varphi(z)r^4/4 + O(r^6)$ and
$\varphi'(u)r^2 = -z\varphi(z)r^2 + z(z^2 - 1)\varphi(z)r^4/2 + O(r^6)$. The terms in $r^2$ cancel, and
the terms in $r^4$ add up to
$\varphi(z)\{-(z + z^3)/4 + z(z^2 - 1)/2 + (3z - z^3)/12\} = z(z^2 - 3)\varphi(z)/6$. For small biases,
the widened interval therefore overcovers if $z > \sqrt 3$ and undercovers if $z < \sqrt 3$; the global
statement for all $r$ is the numerical check above.

The plug-in replaces $b$ by the estimated difference. For a contrast $\mathbf a$, let
$\hat\delta = \mathbf a^\top(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_N - \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_R)$, with biases $b_N$,
$b_R$ and variances $\sigma_N^2$, $\sigma_R^2$, covariance $\sigma_{NR}$ of the two contrasts. Then
$$
\mathrm E\hat\delta^2 = (b_N - b_R)^2 + \sigma_N^2 + \sigma_R^2 - 2\sigma_{NR},
$$
so $\mathrm{se}^2_{\mathrm{CL2},N} + \hat\delta^2$ estimates $\sigma_N^2 + b_N^2$ only if $b_R \approx 0$
and $\sigma_R^2 \approx 2\sigma_{NR}$. Under within-curve dependence, $\sigma_R^2$ is large (REML
undersmooths), which inflates the added term $\hat\delta^2$, while a bias shared by both fits cancels in
$b_N - b_R$.

*Result.* In the synthetic settings with dependent errors and a smooth truth, the widened interval overcovers
$\beta$ (`r f(hv5("dependent, smooth truth", "ncv_cl2_bias", "cov"), 2)`); under the REML-fitted plasmode
truth, it covers `r f(hv5("plasmode, REML-fitted truth", "ncv_cl2_bias", "cov"), 2)` with a lower tail of
`r f(hv5("plasmode, REML-fitted truth", "ncv_cl2_bias", "q05"), 2)` (next table and figure).

*Reason.* The estimated difference is not the bias. It carries REML's sampling variance, which is
large under dependence, so the interval is too wide where REML is noisy; and it cannot see bias that
both fits share, which concentrates where the truth is most curved.

### (c) NCV estimate with the REML + CL2 width

*Method.* Center REML + CL2's pointwise half-width at the NCV estimate.

*Result.* The detection rate of this interval for $\beta$ is lower than REML + CL2's on `r det_lower_n` of 9 plasmode
datasets (`r rng(det_p$hybrid)` against `r rng(det_p$reml_cl2)`). Under the REML-fitted plasmode truth,
it covers `r f(hv5("plasmode, REML-fitted truth", "hybrid", "cov"), 2)` with a lower tail of
`r f(hv5("plasmode, REML-fitted truth", "hybrid", "q05"), 2)` (REML + CL2:
`r f(hv5("plasmode, REML-fitted truth", "reml_cl2", "cov"), 2)`,
`r f(hv5("plasmode, REML-fitted truth", "reml_cl2", "q05"), 2)`). Elsewhere it overcovers:
`r f(hv5("dependent, smooth truth", "hybrid", "cov"), 2)` and `r f(hv5("dependent, rough truth", "hybrid", "cov"), 2)`
in the synthetic settings with dependent errors (smooth and rough truth), and
`r f(hv5("plasmode, NCV-fitted truth", "hybrid", "cov"), 2)` and `r f(hv5("plasmode, midpoint truth", "hybrid", "cov"), 2)`
under the NCV-fitted and the midpoint plasmode truth (next table).

*Reason.* Its width equals REML + CL2's by construction, so a lower interval score only says that the
NCV estimate is closer to the truth, and the wide band around a smoother center excludes zero less
often. Its coverage relies on REML's standard error absorbing NCV's bias: the interval is then
wider than needed where the NCV estimate is accurate, and it covers unevenly under the REML-fitted
truth, the truth least favorable to the NCV fit.

```{r t-s5-hyb}
#| output: asis
stab(hyb_tab_s5 |> rename(combinations = n), "$\\beta(s,t)$: coverage (5% quantile of pointwise coverage) and width / interval score relative to REML + CL2 (geometric means of per-setting ratios). Synthetic: main factorial at $G = 100$ and rough-truth settings with smooth errors; plasmode: all subjects, fitted residuals, by truth source. NCV–REML widening: NCV + CL2 widened in quadrature by the NCV–REML difference.", font = 6.5)
```

```{r f-s5-maps}
#| fig-cap: "Pointwise coverage of $\\beta(s,t)$ for REML + CL2 and three intervals centered at the NCV estimate, Gaussian, default signal, $G = 100$, smooth errors, rough truth (top) and smooth truth (bottom); black contour at 0.90; the color scale ends at 0.7 and values at or below it share its darkest color. Widened: NCV + CL2 widened by the NCV–REML difference; NCV est.: NCV estimate with REML + CL2's half-width. Right: curvature of the truth."
#| fig-height: 3.9
fig_maps <- FIGS[["coverage-maps-synthetic"]]
short_lab <- \(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)
  x[grepl("widened|NCV–REML", x)] <- "NCV + CL2,\nwidened"
  x[grepl("REML \\+ CL2 width|half-width", x)] <- "NCV est.,\nREML + CL2 width"
  x
}
fig_maps[[1]]$data$method <- factor(short_lab(fig_maps[[1]]$data$method), unique(short_lab(levels(factor(fig_maps[[1]]$data$method)))))
sfig_maps(fig_maps)
```

### (d) One-step bias correction

*Method.* For a penalized fit at fixed $\boldsymbol\lambda$ and Gaussian responses,
$\mathrm E\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} = \mathbf A\boldsymbol\theta$ with
$\mathbf A = \mathbf V_e\mathbf V_p^{-1} = \mathbf V_p\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X$. Directions in
which NCV shrinks the estimate almost completely ($\mathbf A \approx \mathbf 0$) carry no information
from the data, so no correction of this kind can restore them. The corrected estimate
$\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta} = (2\mathbf I - \mathbf A)\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ ("twicing", @Tukey1977)
has bias $-(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)^2\boldsymbol\theta$ instead of $-(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)\boldsymbol\theta$.
Its covariance propagates the frequentist CL2 covariance $\mathbf V_f$ through the same map and keeps
the Bayesian smoothing-bias term,
$\mathbf M\mathbf V_f\mathbf M^\top + (\mathbf I - \mathbf A)(\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)^\top$
with $\mathbf M = 2\mathbf I - \mathbf A$, as in robust bias correction [@CalonicoCattaneoFarrell2018].
It needs no refit.

*Derivation: mean and bias.* For Gaussian responses with identity link and fixed $\boldsymbol\lambda$,
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} = \mathbf F^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf y$, so
$\mathrm E\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} = \mathbf F^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\boldsymbol\theta = \mathbf A\boldsymbol\theta$ with
$$
\mathbf A = \mathbf V_p\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X = (\mathbf V_p\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\mathbf V_p)\mathbf V_p^{-1} = \mathbf V_e\mathbf V_p^{-1},
\qquad
\mathbf I - \mathbf A = \mathbf V_p(\mathbf F - \mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X) = \mathbf V_p\mathbf S ,
$$
and the bias is $-(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)\boldsymbol\theta = -\mathbf V_p\mathbf S\boldsymbol\theta$ (Appendix A.3 of
the paper). Twicing applies the estimated bias map to the estimate,
$\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta} = \hat{\boldsymbol\theta} + (\mathbf I - \mathbf A)\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} = (2\mathbf I - \mathbf A)\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$,
with $\mathrm E\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta} = (2\mathbf I - \mathbf A)\mathbf A\boldsymbol\theta = \{\mathbf I - (\mathbf I - \mathbf A)^2\}\boldsymbol\theta$.
Repeating the step $m$ times gives
$\mathbf M_m = \sum_{\ell=0}^{m}(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)^\ell$ and
$\mathrm E\,\mathbf M_m\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} = \{\mathbf I - (\mathbf I - \mathbf A)^{m+1}\}\boldsymbol\theta$; two
steps give $\mathbf M_2 = 3\mathbf I - 3\mathbf A + \mathbf A^2$ with bias $-(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)^3\boldsymbol\theta$.
If $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X$ is invertible, $\mathbf M_m \to \mathbf A^{-1}$ as $m \to \infty$, and
$\mathbf A^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ is the unpenalized estimate. For GLMs, the same algebra holds
for the working linear model at the converged weights, to first order; $\mathbf A$ is computed as
$\mathbf V_e\mathbf V_p^{-1}$ from the fit.

*Derivation: covariance.* At fixed $\boldsymbol\lambda$, $\mathbf M$ is fixed, so
$\mathrm{Var}(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}) = \mathbf M\,\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})\mathbf M^\top$, estimated by
$\mathbf M\mathbf V_f\mathbf M^\top$ with the frequentist CL2. The smoothing-bias allowance follows from the
Bayesian reading of Appendix A.3: under $\boldsymbol\theta \sim N(\mathbf 0, \mathbf S^-)$, the bias
$-(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)\boldsymbol\theta$ of $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ has covariance
$\mathbf V_p\mathbf S\mathbf S^-\mathbf S\mathbf V_p = \mathbf V_p\mathbf S\mathbf V_p = \mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e$,
which is CL2's allowance. The bias of $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}$ is
$-(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)\{(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)\boldsymbol\theta\}$, with prior covariance
$(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)(\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)^\top$; after two steps, it is
$(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)^2(\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)\{(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)^2\}^\top$. The interval uses
$$
\mathbf M\mathbf V_f\mathbf M^\top + (\mathbf I - \mathbf A)(\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)^\top ,
$$
not $\mathbf M\hat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{CL2}}\mathbf M^\top$, which propagates the allowance through the
correction as if it were sampling variance.

*Derivation: directions.* Let
$\mathbf F^{-1/2}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\mathbf F^{-1/2} = \mathbf Q\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf Q^\top$ with
$\boldsymbol\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(a_k)$, $0 \le a_k \le 1$ ($a_k = 1$ in the null space of the
penalty), and $\mathbf B = \mathbf F^{-1/2}\mathbf Q$. Then $\mathbf A\mathbf B = \mathbf B\boldsymbol\Lambda$,
and
$$
\mathbf V_e = \mathbf B\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf B^\top,\quad
\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e = \mathbf B(\mathbf I - \boldsymbol\Lambda)\mathbf B^\top,\quad
(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)(\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)^\top = \mathbf B(\mathbf I - \boldsymbol\Lambda)^3\mathbf B^\top,\quad
\mathbf M(\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)\mathbf M^\top = \mathbf B(2\mathbf I - \boldsymbol\Lambda)^2(\mathbf I - \boldsymbol\Lambda)\mathbf B^\top .
$$
In the coordinates $\boldsymbol\vartheta = \mathbf B^{-1}\boldsymbol\theta$, component $k$ of the estimate
has mean $a_k\vartheta_k$, working-model variance $a_k$ and bias $-(1 - a_k)\vartheta_k$; after twicing,
the mean is $(2 - a_k)a_k\vartheta_k$, the variance $(2 - a_k)^2a_k$ and the bias $-(1 - a_k)^2\vartheta_k$.
The correctly propagated allowance is $(1 - a_k)^3$, smaller than the original $1 - a_k$; propagating the
Bayesian CL2 through $\mathbf M$ gives $(2 - a_k)^2(1 - a_k)$, up to four times the original. In
directions with $a_k \approx 0$, which NCV shrinks almost completely, the estimate carries
almost no information about $\vartheta_k$: any linear correction $p(\mathbf A)\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ has
mean $p(a_k)a_k\vartheta_k$ and variance $p(a_k)^2a_k$, so recovering a fraction $\kappa$ of $\vartheta_k$
needs $p(a_k) = \kappa/a_k$ and a variance $\kappa^2/a_k$ that diverges as $a_k \to 0$. For
$\mathbf M_m$, $p(a) = \{1 - (1 - a)^{m+1}\}/a \le m + 1$, and the bias $-(1 - a_k)^{m+1}\vartheta_k$
stays close to $-\vartheta_k$.

*Result.* On 200 fresh synthetic replicates, the corrected interval covers $\beta$ at
`r f(rsv("smooth truth, Gaussian/Poisson", "rbc_p", "cov"), 2)` (smooth truth, Gaussian and Poisson) and
`r f(rsv("rough truth, Gaussian/Poisson", "rbc_p", "cov"), 2)` (rough truth; NCV + CL2
`r f(rsv("rough truth, Gaussian/Poisson", "ncv_cl2", "cov"), 2)`, REML + CL2
`r f(rsv("rough truth, Gaussian/Poisson", "reml_cl2", "cov"), 2)`), and binary $\beta$ at
`r f(rsv("binary", "rbc_p", "cov"), 2)`. On the plasmode datasets, it adds
`r rng_pp(combo_p$cov[combo_p$arm == "rbc_p"] - combo_p$cov[combo_p$arm == "ncv_cl2"])` to the coverage of NCV + CL2
(figure in (f)).

*Reason.* One step removes only part of the bias, none of it in the directions NCV shrinks
completely, and leaves the smoothing-parameter variability of (a) untouched.

```{r f-s5-rbc}
#| fig-cap: "One-step bias correction, $\\beta(s,t)$, 200 fresh replicates per setting: coverage, lower tail (5% quantile of pointwise coverage), width relative to REML + CL2 (geometric mean), detection rate and median relative error of the center, by group of settings (their number in brackets). Dashed: nominal 0.95 for coverage. Values: S7."
#| fig-height: 2.6
sfig_rbc(rbc_s)
```

### (e) Smoothing-parameter uncertainty term

*Method.* The NCV criterion with curve blocks has analytic derivatives with respect to a weight
$w_i$ on each curve. With the curve scores $\mathbf s_i = \partial^2\mathrm{NCV}/\partial\boldsymbol\rho\,\partial w_i$
($\boldsymbol\rho = \log\boldsymbol\lambda$) and the Hessian $\mathbf H$ of the criterion in
$\boldsymbol\rho$, the infinitesimal jackknife over curves gives the influence
$\mathbf d_i = -\mathbf H^{-1}(\mathbf s_i - \bar{\mathbf s})$ of curve $i$ on $\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}$ and
the curve-robust variance $\hat{\mathbf V}_\rho = \sum_i\mathbf d_i\mathbf d_i^\top$. It enters the
coefficient covariance as $\mathbf J\hat{\mathbf V}_\rho\mathbf J^\top$ with
$\mathbf J = \partial\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}/\partial\boldsymbol\rho$ ("$\lambda$ term"), optionally with
the first-order cross term between the coefficient and the smoothing-parameter influences.

*Derivation: the first-order term.* Let $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}(\boldsymbol\rho)$ be the penalized fit at
fixed $\boldsymbol\rho$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}$ the selected value with limit $\boldsymbol\rho_0$.
Implicit differentiation of the estimating equation $\sum_i\mathbf u_i(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}) = \mathbf S\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$
(Appendix A.1 of the paper) in $\rho_k$ gives $-\mathbf F\,\partial\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}/\partial\rho_k - \dot{\mathbf S}_k\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} = \mathbf 0$,
so the columns of $\mathbf J = \partial\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}/\partial\boldsymbol\rho^\top$ are
$\mathbf J_k = -\mathbf V_p\dot{\mathbf S}_k\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ (mgcv's `db.drho`). To first order,
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}(\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}) - \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}(\boldsymbol\rho_0) \approx \mathbf J(\hat{\boldsymbol\rho} - \boldsymbol\rho_0),
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}(\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}) \approx \mathrm{Var}\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}(\boldsymbol\rho_0) + \mathbf J\,\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\rho})\mathbf J^\top + \mathbf C + \mathbf C^\top ,
$$
with the cross covariance $\mathbf C = \mathrm{Cov}\{\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}(\boldsymbol\rho_0), \hat{\boldsymbol\rho}\}\mathbf J^\top$.
The terms left out (the dependence of $\mathbf V_p$ and $\mathbf J$ on $\boldsymbol\rho$, the curvature of
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}(\boldsymbol\rho)$) are of order $G^{-1}$ relative to the first-order term when
$\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}$ is $\sqrt G$-regular. For the surface penalty under dependence, it is not: the sampling
distribution of $\log\hat\lambda$ is flat or bimodal at $G = 40$, and its SD shrinks by a factor of only
`r f(lcc_shrink, 2)` from $G = 40$ to $G = 100$ (REML; $\sqrt{40/100} = `r f(sqrt(0.4), 2)`$).

*Derivation: mgcv's $\mathbf V_c$.* @WoodPyaSafken2016 argue in the Bayesian model: given $\boldsymbol\rho$,
$\boldsymbol\theta \mid \mathbf y, \boldsymbol\rho \sim N\{\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}(\boldsymbol\rho), \mathbf V_p(\boldsymbol\rho)\}$,
and, with a flat prior, the Laplace approximation gives
$\boldsymbol\rho \mid \mathbf y \approx N(\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}, \mathbf H^{-1})$, with $\mathbf H$ the Hessian of the
negative log restricted likelihood in the outer parameters (block $\boldsymbol\rho\boldsymbol\rho$ of its
inverse, if the scale is estimated). The law of total variance and the linearization
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}(\boldsymbol\rho) \approx \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}(\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}) + \mathbf J(\boldsymbol\rho - \hat{\boldsymbol\rho})$
give $\mathbf V_c = \mathbf V_p + \mathbf J\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf J^\top$, to which mgcv adds a second-order
term. Two working assumptions are built in. First, $\mathbf H^{-1}$ is the variance of
$\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}$ only if the information identity holds, i.e. if the variance of the gradient of
the criterion equals its expected Hessian, which is the case when the $N$ rows are independent with
variance $\phi V(\mu)$. For Gaussian responses, the data enter the $\rho_k$-gradient through
$\tfrac12\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^\top\dot{\mathbf S}_k\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} = \tfrac12\mathbf y^\top\mathbf Q_k\mathbf y$ with
$\mathbf Q_k = \mathbf W\mathbf X\mathbf V_p\dot{\mathbf S}_k\mathbf V_p\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W$; for $\mathrm E\mathbf y = \mathbf m$ and
$\mathrm{Var}\,\mathbf y = \boldsymbol\Sigma$, its variance is
$\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf Q_k\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf Q_k\boldsymbol\Sigma) + \mathbf m^\top\mathbf Q_k\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf Q_k\mathbf m$,
whereas $\mathbf H$ corresponds to $\boldsymbol\Sigma = \phi\mathbf I$. In the main-factorial settings with dependent errors,
mgcv's $\mathbf H^{-1}$ gives standard deviations of the surface penalty's $\log\hat\lambda$ of
`r rng(lcc_naive)` times its Monte Carlo SD (median over replicates; REML). Second, the law of total variance has no cross term: in the Bayesian model,
$\boldsymbol\theta$ given $\boldsymbol\rho$ is the posterior. Over repeated samples with a fixed truth,
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ and the gradient are correlated: for symmetric errors
$\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf y^\top\mathbf Q_k\mathbf y, \mathbf a^\top\mathbf y) = 2\mathbf m^\top\mathbf Q_k\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf a$, so
$\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^\top\dot{\mathbf S}_k\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}, \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}) = 2\mathbf V_p\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf W\mathbf X\mathbf V_p\dot{\mathbf S}_k\,\mathrm E\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$,
which vanishes only if $\dot{\mathbf S}_k\mathrm E\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} = \mathbf 0$.

*Derivation: curve contributions.* Give curve $i$ a weight $c_i$ in the selection criterion
$\mathcal V(\boldsymbol\omega; \mathbf c)$ (in its log-likelihood for REML; in its loss term and in every
fit for NCV), so that $\mathbf c = \mathbf 1$ is the data and $c_i = 0$ deletes the curve;
$\boldsymbol\omega$ collects the outer parameters ($\boldsymbol\rho$, and $\tau = \log\phi$ for a Gaussian
REML fit). The selected value solves $\nabla_{\boldsymbol\omega}\mathcal V(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}; \mathbf c) = \mathbf 0$,
and the implicit-function theorem gives
$$
\frac{d\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}}{dc_i}\Big|_{\mathbf c = \mathbf 1} = -\mathbf H_\omega^{-1}\mathbf s_i,
\qquad
\mathbf s_i = \frac{\partial\nabla_{\boldsymbol\omega}\mathcal V(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}; \mathbf c)}{\partial c_i}\Big|_{\mathbf c = \mathbf 1},
\qquad
\mathbf H_\omega = \nabla^2_{\boldsymbol\omega}\mathcal V ,
$$
where $\mathbf s_i$ is a total derivative that includes the dependence of $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$,
$\mathbf W$ and the leave-out fits on $\mathbf c$. Neither criterion is a sum of curve terms (log
determinants; leave-out fits that use all other curves), so the decomposition
$\hat{\boldsymbol\omega} - \boldsymbol\omega_0 \approx \sum_i\mathbf d_i$ holds only to first order: it is the
influence-function expansion of $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}$ in the curves. The penalty does not scale with
$\mathbf c$, so $\sum_i\mathbf s_i \ne \mathbf 0$. Perturbing the empirical distribution of the curves at
fixed total weight, $\mathbf c = \mathbf 1 + \varepsilon(\mathbf e_i - \mathbf 1/G)$, gives the curve influence
$\mathbf d_i = -\mathbf H_\omega^{-1}(\mathbf s_i - \bar{\mathbf s})$.

*Derivation: estimators of $\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega})$.* (i) The infinitesimal jackknife (IJ),
$$
\hat{\mathbf V}_\omega = \frac{G}{G-1}\sum_i\mathbf d_i\mathbf d_i^\top = \mathbf H_\omega^{-1}\hat{\mathbf M}\mathbf H_\omega^{-1},
\qquad
\hat{\mathbf M} = \frac{G}{G-1}\sum_i(\mathbf s_i - \bar{\mathbf s})(\mathbf s_i - \bar{\mathbf s})^\top,
$$
a sandwich for $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}$ with the curves as clusters. It differs from mgcv's
$\mathbf H^{-1}$ in the meat and agrees with it when $\hat{\mathbf M} = \mathbf H_\omega$. (ii) The one-step
leave-curve-out (OS) estimator: at $\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{(-i)} = \hat{\boldsymbol\theta} - (\mathbf F - \tilde{\mathbf X}_i^\top\tilde{\mathbf X}_i)^{-1}\mathbf u_i$
(exact for Gaussian responses; for GLMs, the start of penalized IRLS at fixed $\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}$, iterated
to convergence), then one Newton step in the outer parameters,
$\boldsymbol\Delta_i = -\mathbf H_\omega^{-1}\{\nabla\mathcal V_{(-i)}(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}) - \nabla\mathcal V(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega})\}$,
with the leave-out gradient evaluated exactly (re-evaluated weights, $\mathbf F$ and number of
observations), and $\hat{\mathbf V}_\omega = \frac{G-1}{G}\sum_i(\boldsymbol\Delta_i - \bar{\boldsymbol\Delta})(\boldsymbol\Delta_i - \bar{\boldsymbol\Delta})^\top$.
Since $\nabla\mathcal V_{(-i)} - \nabla\mathcal V \approx -\mathbf s_i$, $\boldsymbol\Delta_i - \bar{\boldsymbol\Delta} \approx -\mathbf d_i$:
IJ and OS agree to first order, and OS carries the leave-out inflation of the jackknife, as CR3 does
relative to CR0. (iii) The exact curve jackknife, the reference: $\boldsymbol\Delta_i = \hat{\boldsymbol\omega}_{(-i)} - \hat{\boldsymbol\omega}$
from a refit without curve $i$ (same basis, constraints and penalties, warm start), with the same
formula; it needs $G$ refits. (iv) Regularized variants replace $\mathbf H_\omega^{-1}$ by
$(\mathbf H_{\omega,+} + \mathbf I/10)^{-1}$, where $\mathbf H_{\omega,+}$ has its non-positive eigenvalues set
to zero and $1/10$ is the prior precision of mgcv's second-order term. When a smoothing parameter
drifts toward a boundary, $\mathbf H_\omega$ has a small eigenvalue along it and
$\mathbf H_\omega^{-1}\mathbf s_i$ explodes while $\mathbf J$ is nearly zero there; the product is numerically
uncontrolled and produced heavy upper tails of $\hat{\mathbf V}_\rho$ over replicates.

*Derivation: adding the term to CL2.* The influence of curve $i$ on $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}(\hat{\boldsymbol\rho})$
is $\boldsymbol\psi_i = \mathbf k_i + \mathbf J\mathbf d_{i,\rho}$, where $\mathbf d_{i,\rho}$ is the
$\boldsymbol\rho$-block of $\mathbf d_i$ ($\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ does not depend on $\tau$). CL2 replaces the
coefficient part by its leverage-adjusted version $\mathbf k_i$; the $\boldsymbol\rho$-part is not
adjusted. Without the cross term,
$\hat{\mathbf V} = \hat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{CL2}} + \mathbf J\hat{\mathbf V}_\rho\mathbf J^\top$ with
$\hat{\mathbf V}_\rho$ the $\boldsymbol\rho\boldsymbol\rho$-block of $\hat{\mathbf V}_\omega$. With the cross term, the
sandwich of the stacked influences,
$$
\hat{\mathbf V}_\times = \frac{G}{G-1}\sum_i(\mathbf k_i + \mathbf J\mathbf d_{i,\rho})(\mathbf k_i + \mathbf J\mathbf d_{i,\rho})^\top + (\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)
= \hat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{CL2}} + \mathbf J\hat{\mathbf V}_\rho\mathbf J^\top + \frac{G}{G-1}\sum_i(\mathbf k_i\mathbf d_{i,\rho}^\top\mathbf J^\top + \mathbf J\mathbf d_{i,\rho}\mathbf k_i^\top),
$$
the plug-in for $\mathbf C + \mathbf C^\top$ above. For leave-out changes, $\mathbf d_{i,\rho}$ is replaced by
$-(\boldsymbol\Delta_{i,\rho} - \bar{\boldsymbol\Delta}_\rho)$ rescaled by $(G-1)/G$, so that the
$\boldsymbol\rho\boldsymbol\rho$-part equals the jackknife variance in both forms. The result is a CL2-based
hybrid, not a sandwich derived from one estimating equation. Assumptions: independent curves, a
correct mean model, a canonical link with unit prior weights and no offsets, smoothing parameters that
are neither linked nor fixed, a converged fit at an interior optimum with positive definite $\mathbf F$,
and, for the first-order term to be accurate, $\sqrt G$-regular $\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}$.

*Derivation: curve-blocked NCV, Gaussian responses.* With curve weights,
$\mathbf F_{\mathbf c} = \sum_h c_h\tilde{\mathbf X}_h^\top\tilde{\mathbf X}_h + \mathbf S$, the fit without curve $i$ is
$$
\mathbf t_i = \mathbf F_{(-i)}^{-1}\sum_{h \ne i}c_h\mathbf X_h^\top\mathbf W_h\mathbf y_h,
\qquad \mathbf F_{(-i)} = \mathbf F_{\mathbf c} - c_i\tilde{\mathbf X}_i^\top\tilde{\mathbf X}_i ,
$$
and the curve-blocked NCV criterion of §2 of the paper, divided by $\phi$, is
$\mathcal V(\boldsymbol\rho; \mathbf c) = \sum_i c_i\mathbf r_i^\top\mathbf W_i\mathbf r_i$ with
$\mathbf r_i = \mathbf y_i - \mathbf X_i\mathbf t_i$. For Gaussian responses, mgcv's Newton-step leave-out fit is
exact, so the criterion above is mgcv's criterion; the factor $1/\phi$ cancels in $\mathbf H_\rho^{-1}\mathbf s_i$, and there is
no scale parameter among the outer parameters. A zero weight removes curve $i$ from the loss and from every
other leave-out fit. With $\mathbf v_{ik} = \mathbf F_{(-i)}^{-1}\dot{\mathbf S}_k\mathbf t_i$,
$\partial\mathbf t_i/\partial\rho_k = -\mathbf v_{ik}$, and with
$\mathbf u^{\mathrm{cv}}_i = \mathbf F_{(-i)}^{-1}\mathbf X_i^\top\mathbf W_i\mathbf r_i$ and
$q_{ik} = \mathbf u^{\mathrm{cv}\top}_i\dot{\mathbf S}_k\mathbf t_i$,
$$
\frac{\partial\mathcal V}{\partial\rho_k} = 2\sum_i c_i\,q_{ik},
\qquad
H_{\rho,kl} = 2\sum_i c_i\bigl[(\mathbf X_i\mathbf v_{il})^\top\mathbf W_i\mathbf X_i\mathbf v_{ik} + \mathbb 1_{k=l}\,q_{ik} - \mathbf u^{\mathrm{cv}\top}_i\dot{\mathbf S}_l\mathbf v_{ik} - \mathbf u^{\mathrm{cv}\top}_i\dot{\mathbf S}_k\mathbf v_{il}\bigr],
$$
using $\partial\mathbf u^{\mathrm{cv}}_i/\partial\rho_l = \mathbf F_{(-i)}^{-1}(\mathbf X_i^\top\mathbf W_i\mathbf X_i\mathbf v_{il} - \dot{\mathbf S}_l\mathbf u^{\mathrm{cv}}_i)$.
For the curve scores, $\mathbf t_h$ does not depend on $c_h$, and for $i \ne h$
$\partial\mathbf F_{(-i)}/\partial c_h = \tilde{\mathbf X}_h^\top\tilde{\mathbf X}_h$ and
$\partial\mathbf t_i/\partial c_h = \mathbf F_{(-i)}^{-1}\mathbf X_h^\top\mathbf W_h\mathbf e_{h\mid i}$, with
$\mathbf e_{h\mid i} = \mathbf y_h - \mathbf X_h\mathbf t_i$ the residual of curve $h$ under the fit without
$i$. Differentiating $q_{ik}$ gives, with $\mathbf m_{1,ik} = \mathbf F_{(-i)}^{-1}\mathbf X_i^\top\mathbf W_i\mathbf X_i\mathbf v_{ik}$
and $\mathbf m_{2,ik} = \mathbf F_{(-i)}^{-1}\dot{\mathbf S}_k\mathbf u^{\mathrm{cv}}_i$,
$$
s_{hk} = \frac{\partial^2\mathcal V}{\partial\rho_k\,\partial c_h}\Big|_{\mathbf c = \mathbf 1}
= 2q_{hk} + 2\sum_{i \ne h}\bigl[\mathbf e_{h\mid i}^\top\mathbf W_h\mathbf X_h(\mathbf m_{2,ik} - \mathbf m_{1,ik}) - (\mathbf X_h\mathbf u^{\mathrm{cv}}_i)^\top\mathbf W_h\mathbf X_h\mathbf v_{ik}\bigr].
$$
The first term is curve $h$'s own loss, the sum its effect on every other leave-out fit. The cost is
$O(GKNp + Gp^3)$. Since $\mathcal V(\boldsymbol\rho; c\mathbf 1) = c\,\mathcal V(\boldsymbol\rho - \log c; \mathbf 1)$,
$\sum_h\mathbf s_h = \nabla_\rho\mathcal V - \mathbf H_\rho\mathbf 1$, a check of signs and centering that the
implementation meets to $10^{-12}$; scores and Hessian also agree with central differences. NCV is a
prediction loss, not a log-likelihood, so $\mathbf H_\rho^{-1}$ alone is not a covariance of
$\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}$; the IJ sandwich $\mathbf H_\rho^{-1}\hat{\mathbf M}\mathbf H_\rho^{-1}$ is, to first order, and
it is invariant to rescaling the criterion. The regularized variants are not (the prior $1/10$ does not
rescale), so they serve only as a sensitivity check. $\mathbf J$ is the same as for REML, because the
penalized fit at given $\boldsymbol\rho$ is the same.

*Derivation: curve-blocked NCV, Poisson and binary responses.* With a canonical link and $\phi = 1$,
$\mathbf W = \mathrm{diag}(d\mu/d\eta)$ depends on $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$, and mgcv approximates the fit without
curve $i$ by one Newton step from $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$:
$\mathbf F_{(-i)} = \mathbf F - c_i\mathbf X_i^\top\mathbf W_i\mathbf X_i$,
$\boldsymbol\delta_i = \mathbf F_{(-i)}^{-1}\mathbf X_i^\top c_i(\mathbf y_i - \boldsymbol\mu_i)$,
$\boldsymbol\eta_{(-i)} = \mathbf X_i(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} - \boldsymbol\delta_i)$, and
$\mathcal V = \sum_i c_i\sum_j\mathrm{dev}\{y_{ij}, \mu(\eta_{(-i),j})\}$. The derivatives in a direction
$(\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}, \dot{\mathbf c})$ follow by implicit differentiation of the score equation
($d\{c(y - \mu)\}/d\eta = -cw$ for a canonical link); with $\dot{\mathbf S} = \sum_k\dot\rho_k\dot{\mathbf S}_k$,
$w' = dw/d\eta$ and $\circ$ the elementwise product,
$$
\dot{\boldsymbol\theta} = \mathbf F^{-1}\{\mathbf X^\top(\dot{\mathbf c}\circ(\mathbf y - \boldsymbol\mu)) - \dot{\mathbf S}\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\},\quad
\dot{\boldsymbol\eta} = \mathbf X\dot{\boldsymbol\theta},\quad
(\mathbf c\mathbf w)^{\boldsymbol\cdot} = \dot{\mathbf c}\circ\mathbf w + \mathbf c\circ\mathbf w'\circ\dot{\boldsymbol\eta},\quad
\{\mathbf c(\mathbf y - \boldsymbol\mu)\}^{\boldsymbol\cdot} = \dot{\mathbf c}\circ(\mathbf y - \boldsymbol\mu) - \mathbf c\circ\mathbf w\circ\dot{\boldsymbol\eta},
$$
$$
\dot{\mathbf F} = \mathbf X^\top\mathrm{diag}\{(\mathbf c\mathbf w)^{\boldsymbol\cdot}\}\mathbf X + \dot{\mathbf S},\quad
\dot{\boldsymbol\delta}_i = \mathbf F_{(-i)}^{-1}\bigl[\mathbf X_i^\top\{\mathbf c(\mathbf y - \boldsymbol\mu)\}^{\boldsymbol\cdot}_i - \{\dot{\mathbf F} - \mathbf X_i^\top\mathrm{diag}\{(\mathbf c\mathbf w)^{\boldsymbol\cdot}_i\}\mathbf X_i\}\boldsymbol\delta_i\bigr],\quad
\dot{\boldsymbol\eta}_{(-i)} = \mathbf X_i(\dot{\boldsymbol\theta} - \dot{\boldsymbol\delta}_i),
$$
and, since $\partial\,\mathrm{dev}/\partial\eta = -2(y - \mu)$,
$\dot{\mathcal V} = \sum_i\bigl[\dot c_i\sum_j\mathrm{dev}_{ij} - 2c_i\sum_j(y_{ij} - \mu_{(-i),j})\dot\eta_{(-i),j}\bigr]$.
The $K$ directions in $\boldsymbol\rho$ give the gradient (equal to mgcv's), the $G$ directions in
$\mathbf c$ give $\partial\mathcal V/\partial c_h$; $\mathbf H_\rho$ and the scores are central differences in
$\boldsymbol\rho$ (step $10^{-3}$) of these exact first derivatives. Compared with the Gaussian case, the
weights, the Newton step and the leave-out predictions now move with $\boldsymbol\rho$ and $\mathbf c$
through $\hat{\boldsymbol\eta}$, there is no scale parameter, and $\mathbf J_k = -\mathbf V_p\dot{\mathbf S}_k\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$
at the converged weights. A smoothing parameter whose curvature is below $10^{-3}$ times the largest
diagonal entry of $\mathbf H_\rho$ lies on a flat stretch of the criterion ($\lambda_k \to \infty$, the fit
no longer depends on it); as in mgcv's Newton iteration, it is treated as fixed ($d_{i,k} = 0$) and the IJ
uses the sub-matrices of the free components. This rule cannot represent jumps of $\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}$
between interior and boundary solutions.

*Result.* In the main factorial (200 replicates, dependent errors), the term without the cross term
raises NCV + CL2's coverage of $\beta$ from
`r rng(c(lam_sv("gaussian", 40, "cl2"), lam_sv("gaussian", 100, "cl2")))` to
`r rng(c(lam_sv("gaussian", 40, "ij_lin"), lam_sv("gaussian", 100, "ij_lin")))` for Gaussian responses, at
`r rng(c(lam_sv("gaussian", 40, "ij_lin", "wr"), lam_sv("gaussian", 100, "ij_lin", "wr")), 2)` times the
width; for binary responses with 40 curves, it reaches `r f(lam_sv("binomial", 40, "ij_lin"), 2)`. On the
plasmode datasets with independent source curves, it raises the mean coverage of $\beta$ from
`r f(lpv("cl2", "cov"), 2)` to `r f(lpv("ij_lin", "cov"), 2)` (range over combinations
`r rng(c(lpv("ij_lin", "cmin"), lpv("ij_lin", "cmax")))`). Without the cross term, the variance is
closer to the replicate variance (SE/SD `r rng(c2v("ncv_ij", "se_sd"))` per plasmode dataset, against
`r rng(c2v("ncv_ijx", "se_sd"))` with it) and coverage is lower by
`r rng_pp(c2_gap$cross_gain)` per dataset (second figure in (f)).

*Reason.* The term addresses only the variance part of (a), not the smoothing bias. For binary
responses, the selected smoothing parameters jump between interior and boundary solutions, which a
first-order term cannot represent.

```{r t-s5-lam}
#| output: asis
stab(lam_syn_tab, "Smoothing-parameter uncertainty term for curve-blocked NCV, $\\beta(s,t)$, main-factorial settings with dependent errors at the default signal (200 replicates): coverage (5% quantile of pointwise coverage) and width relative to NCV + CL2. $\\lambda$ fixed: refit at the geometric-mean NCV smoothing parameters of the setting, computed from the same replicates (a diagnostic).", font = 7)
```

### (f) Bias correction and smoothing-parameter term combined

*Method.* Propagate the smoothing-parameter term of (e) through the bias-correction map of (d)
(Gaussian responses only), with or without the cross term. The map $\mathbf M = 2\mathbf I - \mathbf A$ is
held fixed at $\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}$: the construction is a *frozen-map approximation* that ignores
$\partial\mathbf A/\partial\boldsymbol\rho$ (derivation below).

*Derivation.* The corrected estimate is $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}(\hat{\boldsymbol\rho}) = \mathbf M(\hat{\boldsymbol\rho})\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}(\hat{\boldsymbol\rho})$.
For Gaussian responses, $\partial\mathbf V_p/\partial\rho_k = -\mathbf V_p\dot{\mathbf S}_k\mathbf V_p$, so
$\partial\mathbf A/\partial\rho_k = \partial(\mathbf I - \mathbf V_p\mathbf S)/\partial\rho_k = -\mathbf V_p\dot{\mathbf S}_k\mathbf A$ and
$$
\frac{\partial\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}}{\partial\rho_k} = \mathbf M\mathbf J_k - \frac{\partial\mathbf A}{\partial\rho_k}\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}
= \mathbf M\mathbf J_k + \mathbf V_p\dot{\mathbf S}_k\mathbf A\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} .
$$
The second term, $-(\partial\mathbf A/\partial\rho_k)\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$, is first order in the same
smoothing-parameter perturbation as the first. The frozen-map construction keeps the first term only:
the curve influences on $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}$ are taken as
$\mathbf M(\mathbf k_i + \mathbf J\mathbf d_{i,\rho})$, so the coefficient–smoothing-parameter cross term
also uses $\mathbf J = \partial\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}/\partial\boldsymbol\rho$ and not
$\partial\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}/\partial\boldsymbol\rho$. The covariance is
$\mathbf M\mathbf V_{f,\rho}\mathbf M^\top + (\mathbf I - \mathbf A)(\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)^\top$, where
$\mathbf V_{f,\rho}$ is the frequentist CL2 plus the term of (e), with or without the cross term, and
the allowance is propagated as in (d). With two steps, $\mathbf M_2$ and $(\mathbf I - \mathbf A)^2$ replace
$\mathbf M$ and $\mathbf I - \mathbf A$.

*Result.* On 100 fresh synthetic replicates per setting, the version with the cross term covers
$\beta$ at `r f(csv_("smooth truth, Gaussian", "rbc_p_ijx", "cov"), 2)` on smooth truths and
`r f(csv_("rough truth, Gaussian", "rbc_p_ijx", "cov"), 2)` on rough truths, at
`r f(csv_("smooth truth, Gaussian", "rbc_p_ijx", "wr"), 2)` and
`r f(csv_("rough truth, Gaussian", "rbc_p_ijx", "wr"), 2)` times REML + CL2's width, with
SE/SD `r rng(c(csv_("smooth truth, Gaussian", "rbc_p_ijx", "se_sd"), csv_("rough truth, Gaussian", "rbc_p_ijx", "se_sd")), 2)`;
without the cross term, it covers `r f(c2s("rbc_p_ij", "smooth"), 2)` and `r f(c2s("rbc_p_ij", "wiggly"), 2)`.

On the
plasmode data, the combined construction was run on replicates 1--50 of each plasmode combination; REML + CL2 comes
from replicates 1--100 of the bias-correction run on the same combinations. The comparison is
therefore only partly paired, and small differences are descriptive, not evidence of equivalence or
of a precise ranking. The combined construction covers $\beta$ at
`r rng(cpv("rbc_p_ijx", "cov"))` on the datasets with independent source curves (REML + CL2
`r rng(reml_p_app$cov[reml_p_app$app %in% APP_COUNTED])`) at `r rng(cpv("rbc_p_ijx", "wr"), 2)` times
the width, with lower tails `r rng(cpv("rbc_p_ijx", "q05"))` (REML + CL2
`r rng(reml_p_app$q05[reml_p_app$app %in% APP_COUNTED])`), and `r rng(cpv("rbc_p_ijx", "cov", "stress test"))`
on the datasets with dependent source curves. By truth source, coverage is `r f(combo_truth$cov[combo_truth$truth == "REML"], 2)`
(REML-fitted), `r f(combo_truth$cov[combo_truth$truth == "MID"], 2)` (midpoint truth, smoothing parameters at the geometric mean of the REML and NCV values),
`r f(combo_truth$cov[combo_truth$truth == "NCV"], 2)` (NCV-fitted). Without the cross term, it covers
`r rng(c2v("rbc_p_ij", "cov", "counted"))` on the datasets with independent source curves and stays below 0.85 on
`r paste(app_lab(as.character(c2_fail$app)), collapse = ", ")`. Of the `r combo_missing_p$tasks`
plasmode replicate fits, `r combo_missing_p$miss` failed the internal consistency check of the
smoothing-parameter derivatives; they are reported as missing, not replaced.

*Reason.* On synthetic data, the excess variance of the term offsets the bias the correction leaves
(SE/SD above 1). On the plasmode data, the remaining bias is larger, and this construction offers no
width advantage over REML + CL2 while its lower tails are worse. The conclusion is about the
frozen-map approximation evaluated here; whether the full derivative, including
$-(\partial\mathbf A/\partial\boldsymbol\rho)\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$, would change it was not studied.

```{r t-s5-combo-s}
#| output: asis
stab(combo_s_tab |> rename(settings = n), "Synthetic, Gaussian, dependent errors, $\\beta(s,t)$, 100 fresh replicates: coverage (5% quantile of pointwise coverage) and width relative to REML + CL2 for NCV + CL2, with the smoothing-parameter term, with the bias correction, and with both.", font = 6.5)
```

Dashed: nominal 0.95 for coverage, 1 for the ratio. Values: S7."
```{r f-s5-combo-p}
#| fig-height: 4.4
sfig_cells(combo_p_tab, "width relative to REML + CL2")
```

Dashed: nominal 0.95 for coverage, 1 for the ratio. Values: S7."

### (g) Truths outside the spline space

*Method.* We evaluate NCV + CL2 and the corrections of (d)--(f), including their two-step versions, on the
misspecified truths of S5.1 (default basis, 100 replicates).

*Result.* For T2 (the smooth truth plus $\sum_{k=12}^{16}\sqrt 2\cos(k\pi s)\sin(\pi t)$; S5.1), whose missing part loads on directions the covariates barely excite, every
NCV-centered interval covers $\beta(s,t)$ at `r rng(c2m("T2", c("iid", "fpc")))`. For T1 (the smooth truth plus a local Gaussian bump)
under independent errors, they cover `r rng(c2m("T1", "iid"))` with lower tails
`r rng(c2m("T1", "iid", "coverage_q05"))`.

*Reason.* A bias that the spline space cannot represent is invisible to every estimate the corrections
are built from, including the frozen-map combination of (f).

## S4.2 mgcv's neighborhood covariance for curve-blocked NCV

*Method.* mgcv offers a covariance for NCV fits that accounts for the neighborhood structure
(help page `?NCV`, @Wood2024). Computed correctly for curve neighborhoods, it was evaluated on the
same NCV fits as NCV + CL2: in three main-factorial settings (Gaussian, Poisson, binary; smooth
errors, $G = 100$, default signal; replicates 1--`r max(JF_S$n_rep)`) and in the
`r n_distinct(JF_P$cell)` plasmode combinations of the six datasets with independent source curves
(all subjects, curve flips, every truth × residual pair; replicates 1--`r max(JF_P$n_rep)`).

*Derivation: what mgcv computes.* The description follows `?NCV`, @Wood2024 and the source of mgcv
1.9-5 (functions `gam.outer` and `neicov`). mgcv specifies NCV per observation: each observation $n$
is predicted from the fit with a set $\alpha(n)$ of observations dropped. For each $n$, mgcv computes
the change of the coefficients when $n$ alone is left out, $\mathbf d_n = \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{-n} - \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$,
by one Newton step at the selected $\boldsymbol\lambda$, multiplied by $\{(N - 1)/N\}^{0.4}$. To first
order, $\mathbf d_n \approx -\mathbf V_p\tilde{\mathbf x}_nz_n$ (Appendix A.1 of the paper). The
neighborhood-aware estimator is
$$
\hat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{nei}} = \frac{N}{N - \tau}\sum_{n=1}^N\tilde{\mathbf d}_n\Bigl(\sum_{m \in \alpha(n)}\tilde{\mathbf d}_m\Bigr)^{\!\top}
\quad\text{(symmetrized)},
\qquad \tilde{\mathbf d}_n = \mathbf d_n\,\frac{r^{\mathrm{cv}}_n}{r_n},
$$
with $\tau$ the effective degrees of freedom and $r^{\mathrm{cv}}_n/r_n$ the ratio of the cross-validated to
the ordinary deviance residual. mgcv returns
$\hat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{nei}} + a(\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)$, projected onto the positive semidefinite
matrices, where $a = \max\{\operatorname{tr}\hat{\mathbf V}^{(0)}_{\mathrm{nei}}/\operatorname{tr}\mathbf V_e, 1\}$
and $\hat{\mathbf V}^{(0)}_{\mathrm{nei}}$ is the same sum with $\mathbf d_n$ in place of $\tilde{\mathbf d}_n$.
If $\alpha(n)$ is the curve of observation $n$, the sum equals $\frac{N}{N-\tau}\sum_i\mathbf D_i\mathbf D_i^\top$ with
$\mathbf D_i = \sum_{n \in i}\tilde{\mathbf d}_n \approx -\mathbf V_p\tilde{\mathbf X}_i^\top\mathbf z_i$: a curve-cluster
sandwich of CR0 type with the penalized bread and without CL2's leverage adjustment, plus a
rescaled smoothing-bias allowance $a(\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)$. With `nei$jackknife = TRUE`, mgcv instead
returns the jackknife over the folds,
$\sum_i\{(N - D_i)/N\}^{0.8}\mathbf d_i\mathbf d_i^\top + a'(\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)$, with $\mathbf d_i$
the one-step change when curve $i$ is left out and $a' = \operatorname{tr}(\cdot)/\operatorname{tr}\mathbf V_e$ of
the first sum.

*The block specification.* refund specifies the same NCV criterion in block form: $G$ folds, each
dropping and predicting a whole curve. Both forms select the same smoothing parameters and give the
same coefficients, but mgcv 1.9-5 computes its covariance only for the per-observation form. For the
block form, it returns the Bayesian $\mathbf V_p$ when `jackknife` is unset. With `jackknife = TRUE`, its
routine `nei_cov()` reads the $N \times p$ matrix of the changes $\mathbf d_n$ with row stride $G$, so it
uses the wrong entries: the sum has a trace of about $10^{-3}$ times $\operatorname{tr}\mathbf V_e$ or less,
$a = 1$, and the returned covariance is $\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e$, the smoothing-bias allowance alone.
Its standard errors relative to the Bayesian ones are
$\{\mathbf a^\top(\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)\mathbf a/\mathbf a^\top\mathbf V_p\mathbf a\}^{1/2} < 1$ for every contrast
$\mathbf a$ with $\mathbf a^\top\mathbf V_e\mathbf a > 0$. This returned covariance explains the result of `jackknife = TRUE` in the three
synthetic settings (`r max(jack_s5$reps)` replicates): standard errors `r rng(jkv("jack_Vp", "ser"))`
times the Bayesian ones and coverage of the mean and $\beta(s,t)$ of `r rng(jkv("jack_Vp"))`. The
correction will be part of a forthcoming mgcv release.

*Corrected computation.* The function `jackfix_vcov()` (code archive, `ncv-jack-recheck/jackfix-lib.R`)
computes from the block fit what mgcv returns for the per-observation form with $\alpha(n)$ = the curve
of $n$: the single-observation Newton changes, the residual ratios at the leave-curve-out fit, both
sums, $a$ and $a'$. It needs no refit and takes about `r f(median(c(JF_SI$time_jack, JF_PI$time_jack)), 0)` s
per study fit (median), about as long as CL2. In small examples, it reproduces mgcv's covariance for the
per-observation form to a relative difference of $10^{-14}$ (Gaussian) and $10^{-12}$ (Poisson); its
leave-curve-out steps agree with exact leave-one-curve-out refits at fixed smoothing parameters to
$10^{-13}$ for Gaussian responses and to within a few percent for Poisson responses (one Newton step).
At study scale (study setting 12: Gaussian responses, smooth errors, $G = 100$, default signal; replicate 1), a pffr fit with per-observation neighborhoods selects the same
smoothing parameters (largest difference in $\log\lambda$: `r f(max(JF_PW$max_abs_diff_log_sp), 0)`), and
`jackfix_vcov()` of the block fit reproduces its $\mathbf V_p$ and $\mathbf V_c$ to a relative difference of
`r sprintf("%.1e", max(JF_PW$reldiff_Vp, JF_PW$reldiff_Vc))`. The per-observation fit took
`r f(JF_PW$time_pointwise_fit, 0)` s against `r f(JF_PW$time_block_fit, 0)` s for the block fit (one fit each, timed
in a separate run, not comparable with the benchmark times of Appendix C of
the paper). The NCV and
REML estimates and CL2 standard errors of the re-evaluation reproduce the study's records (largest
absolute difference `r sprintf("%.0e", max(JF_CRN[, c("est_NCV", "se_cl2_NCV", "est_REML", "se_cl2_REML")]))`).
No replicate fit failed (`r sum(JF_FAIL$n_fail)` failures).

*Result.* On synthetic data (next table), the corrected covariance is conservative: it covers $\beta$ at
`r rng(jf_sv("jk_nei", "beta"))` (NCV + CL2 `r rng(jf_sv("ncv_cl2", "beta"))`, REML + CL2
`r rng(jf_sv("reml_cl2", "beta"))`) with SE/SD `r rng(jf_sv("jk_nei", "beta", "se_sd"), 2)`, at
`r rng(jf_sv("jk_nei", "beta", "width_vs_ncv_cl2"), 2)` times NCV + CL2's width and
`r rng(jf_sv("jk_nei", "beta", "width_vs_reml_cl2"), 2)` times REML + CL2's. Its sampling part alone
behaves like CL2 (SE/SD for $\beta$ `r rng(jf_sv("jk_cv", "beta", "se_sd"), 2)`). The median of $a$ is
`r rng(JF_SI$alpha_nei, 1)` per setting, so the bias allowance $a(\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e)$ adds a large
term. For binary responses, the corrected covariance covers the mean, $\alpha(t)$ and $\gamma(t)$ at
`r rng(jf_sv("jk_nei", c("mean", "alpha", "gamma"), fam = "binomial"))`, below REML + CL2
(`r rng(jf_sv("reml_cl2", c("mean", "alpha", "gamma"), fam = "binomial"))`). The variant with the
$\hat\lambda$ correction and mgcv's `jackknife = TRUE` estimate differ from it by at most
`r f(max(abs(c(JF_S$coverage[JF_S$arm == "jk_nei_vc"] - JF_S$coverage[JF_S$arm == "jk_nei"], JF_S$coverage[JF_S$arm == "jk_raw"] - JF_S$coverage[JF_S$arm == "jk_nei"]))), 3)` in coverage.

On the plasmode data, over the `r jf_pa("jk_nei", "cells")` combinations, the corrected covariance covers $\beta$ at
`r f(jf_pa("jk_nei"), 2)` on average (5% quantile `r f(jf_pa("jk_nei", "q05"), 2)`, lowest combination
`r f(jf_pa("jk_nei", "min"), 2)`), against `r f(jf_pa("ncv_cl2"), 2)` (`r f(jf_pa("ncv_cl2", "q05"), 2)`) for
NCV + CL2 and `r f(jf_pa("reml_cl2"), 2)` (`r f(jf_pa("reml_cl2", "q05"), 2)`) for REML + CL2, at
`r f(jf_pa("jk_nei", "w2"), 2)` times REML + CL2's width (geometric mean). By truth source, averaged over the `r jf_p_truth("MID", "cells")` combinations of each, it covers $\beta$ at `r f(jf_p_truth("REML"), 2)` under the REML-fitted truth, `r f(jf_p_truth("MID"), 2)` under the midpoint truth and `r f(jf_p_truth("NCV"), 2)` under the NCV-fitted truth. Per dataset, it raises the
coverage of NCV + CL2 for $\beta$ by `r rng(jf_pb$jk_nei - jf_pb$ncv_cl2, 2)` and stays below REML + CL2 on
`r if (all(jf_pb$jk_nei < jf_pb$reml_cl2)) "every dataset" else paste(sum(jf_pb$jk_nei < jf_pb$reml_cl2), "of", nrow(jf_pb), "datasets")`
(by `r rng(jf_pb$reml_cl2 - jf_pb$jk_nei, 3)`).

*Reason.* Computed correctly, mgcv's neighborhood covariance is a curve-cluster sandwich plus a
smoothing-bias allowance that is several times $\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e$. On synthetic data, this
allowance makes the intervals conservative. On the plasmode data, they still undercover. Residual
smoothing bias of the NCV estimate is a plausible contributor (S4.1(a)), which a covariance alone does
not remove; variance and tail-calibration errors are not excluded (SE/SD `r f(jfsd("ecg_roahd"), 2)` on
ECG 8-lead and `r f(jfsd("running"), 2)` on running; second table below). No unique cause of the failure to reach nominal coverage on
these data was established.

```{r t-s5-jack}
#| output: asis
stab(jf_syn_tab, "Intervals for the curve-blocked NCV fit (synthetic, smooth errors, $G = 100$, 100 replicates): coverage (5% quantile of pointwise coverage), SE/SD [width relative to NCV + CL2 / REML + CL2]. Bayesian Vp, NCV + CL2 and the corrected neighborhood covariance use the same NCV fit; REML + CL2 the REML fit to the same data.", font = 5.5, long = TRUE)
```

```{r t-s5-jack-p}
#| output: asis
stab(jf_p_tab, "Plasmode, six datasets with independent source curves, all subjects, 100 replicates per combination: coverage (5% quantile of pointwise coverage) SE/SD [width relative to NCV + CL2 / REML + CL2], means over each dataset's truth × residual combinations (SE/SD: median; widths: geometric mean).", font = 5.5)
```

## S4.3 Smoothing-parameter uncertainty term for REML

*Method.* The analogous term for REML uses curve weights in mgcv's REML criterion: the implicit-function
theorem gives each curve's influence on $(\log\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}, \log\hat\phi)$ through analytic
curve scores, and the infinitesimal jackknife over curves gives a curve-robust variance that enters as
$\mathbf J\hat{\mathbf V}_\rho\mathbf J^\top$ on top of CL2.

*Derivation: criterion and gradient.* With curve weights $c_i$ on the log-likelihood contributions
(including their normalizing constants), $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}(\boldsymbol\rho, \mathbf c)$ maximizes
$\ell_{\mathbf c}(\boldsymbol\theta) - \tfrac12\boldsymbol\theta^\top\mathbf S\boldsymbol\theta$ with
$\ell_{\mathbf c} = \sum_i c_i\ell_i$, and mgcv's Laplace-approximate REML criterion [@Wood2011] is, up to a
constant that depends on neither $\boldsymbol\omega$ nor $\mathbf c$,
$$
\mathcal V(\boldsymbol\omega; \mathbf c) = -\ell_{\mathbf c}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}) + \tfrac12\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^\top\mathbf S\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}
+ \tfrac12\log\lvert\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W_{\mathbf c}\mathbf X + \mathbf S\rvert - \tfrac12\log\lvert\mathbf S\rvert_+ ,
$$
with $\mathbf W_{\mathbf c} = \mathrm{diag}(c_{i(n)}w_n)$, $M_p$ the dimension of the null space of the
penalty, $\boldsymbol\omega = (\boldsymbol\rho, \tau)$ with $\tau = \log\phi$ for Gaussian responses and
$\boldsymbol\omega = \boldsymbol\rho$, $\phi = 1$ for Poisson and binary responses. For Gaussian responses,
$-\ell_{\mathbf c} = \mathcal D_{\mathbf c}/(2\phi) + (N_{\mathbf c}/2)\log(2\pi\phi)$ with the weighted residual sum
of squares $\mathcal D_{\mathbf c}$ and $N_{\mathbf c} = \sum_i c_iD_i$. Write
$\mathbf F_{\mathbf c} = \mathbf X^\top\mathbf W_{\mathbf c}\mathbf X + \mathbf S$. Because $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ maximizes the
penalized log-likelihood, its derivative does not enter the first two terms (envelope theorem), and
$$
\frac{\partial\mathcal V}{\partial\rho_k} = \tfrac12\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^\top\dot{\mathbf S}_k\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}
+ \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf F_{\mathbf c}^{-1}\dot{\mathbf F}_k) - \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf S^+\dot{\mathbf S}_k),
\qquad
\dot{\mathbf F}_k = \dot{\mathbf S}_k + \mathbf X^\top\mathrm{diag}(c_{i(n)}w'_n\,\mathbf x_n^\top\mathbf J_k)\mathbf X ,
$$
$$
\frac{\partial\mathcal V}{\partial\tau} = -\frac12\Bigl(\frac{\mathcal D_{\mathbf c}}{\phi} + \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^\top\mathbf S\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\Bigr) + \frac{N_{\mathbf c} - M_p}{2}
\quad\text{(Gaussian)},
$$
where $w'_n = dw_n/d\eta_n$ (zero for Gaussian responses), $\mathbf x_n^\top$ is row $n$ of $\mathbf X$
and $\mathbf J_k = -\mathbf F_{\mathbf c}^{-1}\dot{\mathbf S}_k\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$. In the $\tau$-derivative,
$\mathbf S = \sum_k(\lambda_k/\phi)\mathbf S_k$ moves with $\phi$ at fixed $\boldsymbol\lambda$, and the two
log-determinants contribute $-p/2$ and $(p - M_p)/2$. $\mathbf H_\omega$ is mgcv's Hessian of this
criterion.

*Derivation: curve scores.* At $\mathbf c = \mathbf 1$, the fixed-$\boldsymbol\lambda$ influence of curve $i$ on
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ is $\boldsymbol\delta_i = \partial\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}/\partial c_i = \mathbf V_p\mathbf u_i$ (implicit
differentiation of $\sum_h c_h\mathbf u_h = \mathbf S\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$), and
$\partial\mathbf F/\partial c_i = \mathbf X^\top\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf b_i)\mathbf X$ with
$b_{i,n} = \mathbb 1[n \in i]\,w_n + w'_n\,\mathbf x_n^\top\boldsymbol\delta_i$. With
$h_n = \mathbf x_n^\top\mathbf V_p\mathbf x_n$, $q_{kn} = \mathbf x_n^\top\mathbf V_p\dot{\mathbf F}_k\mathbf V_p\mathbf x_n$ and
$\tilde{\mathbf a} = \mathbf V_p\mathbf X^\top(\mathbf w'\circ\mathbf h)$, differentiating the three parts of
$\partial\mathcal V/\partial\rho_k$ in $c_i$ gives
$$
s_{i,\rho_k} = \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^\top\dot{\mathbf S}_k\boldsymbol\delta_i
+ \tfrac12\Bigl[-\sum_n b_{i,n}q_{kn} + \sum_{n \in i}w'_n(\mathbf x_n^\top\mathbf J_k)h_n
+ \sum_n w''_n(\mathbf x_n^\top\boldsymbol\delta_i)(\mathbf x_n^\top\mathbf J_k)h_n
- \sum_n b_{i,n}(\mathbf x_n^\top\tilde{\mathbf a})(\mathbf x_n^\top\mathbf J_k) - \tilde{\mathbf a}^\top\dot{\mathbf S}_k\boldsymbol\delta_i\Bigr],
$$
$$
s_{i,\tau} = -\frac{\lVert\mathbf y_i - \boldsymbol\mu_i\rVert^2}{2\phi} + \frac{D_i}{2}\quad\text{(Gaussian)}.
$$
The first term of $s_{i,\rho_k}$ is the route through $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^\top\dot{\mathbf S}_k\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$. The
bracket is the route through $\log\lvert\mathbf F\rvert$: the trace term changes with $\mathbf c$ through
$\mathbf F^{-1}$ (first sum), through the weights of curve $i$ and their change with $\hat{\boldsymbol\eta}$
(second and third sums), and through $\mathbf J_k$, whose derivative is
$\partial\mathbf J_k/\partial c_i = -\mathbf V_p\mathbf X^\top\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf b_i)\mathbf X\mathbf J_k - \mathbf V_p\dot{\mathbf S}_k\boldsymbol\delta_i$
(last two terms). For Gaussian responses, only the first sum remains; it varies over curves because
their designs $\mathbf X_i$ differ (functional covariates). The scale enters through the curve's share of
the residual sum of squares and of $N$. The cost is $O(GNp + KNp^2)$ per fit. The penalty and $M_p$ do not scale with $\mathbf c$, so the scores are centered as in S4.1(e), and the
estimators (IJ, OS, exact curve jackknife, regularized) and the two ways of adding the term to CL2 are
those of S4.1(e). For Poisson and binary responses, OS evaluates the leave-out gradient at the converged
penalized IRLS solution without curve $i$.

*Derivation: non-linear variants.* Because $\mathrm{Var}(\log\hat\lambda)$ of the surface penalty is large and
far from normal under dependence, $\mathbf J\boldsymbol\Delta_{i,\rho}$ can be a poor approximation of the change
of $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$. The non-linear variants replace it by
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{(-i)}(\hat{\boldsymbol\rho} + \boldsymbol\Delta_{i,\rho}) - \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{(-i)}(\hat{\boldsymbol\rho})$, refitted by
penalized IRLS at fixed smoothing parameters, for the one-step and the exact jackknife changes.

*Result.* In the main-factorial settings with dependent errors, the term raises REML + CL2's coverage of $\beta(s,t)$ from `r f(lc_v("cl2", g = 40), 2)` to `r f(lc_v("ij_lin", g = 40), 2)`
($G = 40$) and from `r f(lc_v("cl2", g = 100), 2)` to `r f(lc_v("ij_lin", g = 100), 2)` ($G = 100$), at
`r rng(c(lc_v("ij_lin", "wr", g = 40), lc_v("ij_lin", "wr", g = 100)), 2)` times the width, with interval
score ratios `r rng(c(lc_v("ij_lin", "sr", g = 40), lc_v("ij_lin", "sr", g = 100)), 3)`. The within-setting rank correlation between a replicate's
standard-error inflation and CL2's share of missed grid points in that replicate is
`r f(lc_target$m[lc_target$G == 40], 2)` at $G = 40$ and `r f(lc_target$m[lc_target$G == 100], 2)` at
$G = 100$. As a diagnostic, a refit with the smoothing parameters fixed at the setting's
geometric-mean REML value, computed from the same replicates, is narrower than CL2 and covers better
(`r f(lc_v("fix", g = 40), 2)`, interval score ratio `r f(lc_v("fix", "sr", g = 40), 2)` at $G = 40$); it
changes both the typical amount of smoothing and its variability, so it does not separate the two.

On the plasmode data, the term
raises REML + CL2's coverage of $\beta$ by `r rng_pp(lcp_w$gain)` per combination at interval score
ratios `r rng(lcp_w$sr, 2)`.

*Reason.* The term raises coverage but not the interval score: the added width is not concentrated
in the replicates where CL2 misses (the rank correlation above is negative or near zero), so coverage
rises at about the cost of the added width. These results do not exclude a variance contribution to CL2's
shortfall; they show that this first-order term does not target it.

```{r t-s5-lc}
#| output: asis
stab(lc_tab, "Smoothing-parameter terms for REML + CL2, main-factorial settings with dependent errors at the default signal (200 replicates): coverage, then width / interval score relative to CL2. mgcv's term: mgcv's smoothing-parameter correction added to CL2. $\\lambda$ fixed: refit at the setting's geometric-mean REML smoothing parameters, computed from the same replicates (a diagnostic).", font = 6.5)
```

# S5 Misspecified truths and basis size {#sec-s6}

## S5.1 Truths outside the spline space

Three truths are scored against the exact functions, not their basis projections (Gaussian,
$R^2 = 0.5$, $D = 61$, `r max(MS$n_rep, na.rm = TRUE)` replicates): T0 the study's smooth $\beta(s,t)$
(control); T1 = T0 plus a two-dimensional Gaussian bump (SD 0.05, center (0.3, 0.6)); T2 = T0 plus
$\sum_{k=12}^{16}\sqrt 2\cos(k\pi s)\sin(\pi t)$, directions the covariates barely excite. Each feature
carries 20% of the $\beta$-term signal. Settings: truth × errors and $G$ {independent errors with $G = 100$,
smooth errors with $G = 100$, smooth errors with $G = 40$} × basis {default; 4× finer knots: surface $23 \times 31$, $k = 39$ along $t$}. The bump
region is the set of grid points within two SDs of the bump center.

For the control T0, scoring against the exact function instead of its projection changes nothing of note: with the
default basis, REML + CL2 covers $\beta$ at
`r rng(MS$coverage[MS$truth_label == "T0" & MS$basis == "default" & MS$error == "fpc" & MS$estimand == "beta" & MS$arm == "reml_cl2"])`
under smooth errors.
With the default basis, approximation bias breaks every interval under T2 (REML + CL2 covers $\beta$, over the three error and $G$ settings, at
`r rng(MS$coverage[MS$truth_label == "T2" & MS$basis == "default" & MS$estimand == "beta" & MS$arm == "reml_cl2"])`,
NCV + CL2 at `r rng(MS$coverage[MS$truth_label == "T2" & MS$basis == "default" & MS$estimand == "beta" & MS$arm == "ncv_cl2"])`)
and inside T1's bump (REML + CL2
`r rng(MS$coverage_bump[MS$truth_label == "T1" & MS$basis == "default" & MS$estimand == "beta" & MS$arm == "reml_cl2"])`).
With the basis with 4× finer knots and dependent (smooth) errors, REML + CL2 recovers: $\beta$
`r rng(MS$coverage[MS$truth_label != "T0" & MS$basis == "xlarge" & MS$error == "fpc" & MS$estimand == "beta" & MS$arm == "reml_cl2"])`,
bump region `r rng(MS$coverage_bump[MS$truth_label == "T1" & MS$basis == "xlarge" & MS$error == "fpc" & MS$estimand == "beta" & MS$arm == "reml_cl2"])`.
NCV + CL2 stays biased (T2, smooth errors:
`r rng(MS$coverage[MS$truth_label == "T2" & MS$basis == "xlarge" & MS$error == "fpc" & MS$estimand == "beta" & MS$arm == "ncv_cl2"])`).
REML's coverage with the finer basis comes at the cost of noisy estimates: its mean squared error for $\beta$ under
smooth errors is `r rng(MS$mse[MS$basis == "xlarge" & MS$error == "fpc" & MS$estimand == "beta" & MS$arm == "reml_cl2"], 1)`
against `r rng(MS$mse[MS$basis == "xlarge" & MS$error == "fpc" & MS$estimand == "beta" & MS$arm == "ncv_cl2"], 2)`
for NCV.

Under independent errors, the finer basis does not restore REML + CL2 (T2 $\beta$
`r f(msv("T2", "iid", 100, "xlarge", "beta", "reml_cl2"), 2)`). Coverage of $\alpha(t)$ and $\gamma(t)$ is unaffected
(REML + CL2 `r rng(MS$coverage[MS$estimand %in% c("alpha", "gamma") & MS$arm == "reml_cl2"])`).
